https://render.com Render 2026-11-21T16:10:29.467Z https://github.com/jpmonette/feed Changelog for Render https://cdn.sanity.io/images/hvk0tap5/production/0ea63c1b6854bd803489557afb4ea54b85239418-128x128.png?fit=max&auto=format All rights reserved 2026, Render <![CDATA[Fine-grained API keys now generally available]]> https://render.com/changelog/fine-grained-api-keys-now-generally-available 2026-11-18T00:00:00.000Z Newly created Render API keys are now scoped to a single workspace and can be assigned fine-grained access permissions:

For example, you can grant a key different permission levels for:

  • Services and their deploys
  • Environment variables and secret files
  • Workflows and their task runs
  • Sandboxes and their snapshots
  • Logs, metrics, and service events

Any permission you grant an API key must be allowed by your member role in the workspace.

API keys created before this release have access to every workspace you belong to, with permissions matching your member role.

Learn more about API keys in the documentation.

]]> <![CDATA[Create separate service previews and preview environments for stacked PRs]]> https://render.com/changelog/create-separate-service-previews-and-preview-environments-for-stacked-prs 2026-11-18T00:00:00.000Z You can now create service previews and preview environments for each pull request in a GitHub PR stack:

Previously, Render created previews only for PRs that directly targeted your service's linked branch, so only the bottom PR in a stack could generate previews.

Render now applies your preview mode to all PRs in a stack:

  • Automatic: Render creates previews for each PR in the stack, except for any that include [skip preview] in their title.
  • Manual: Render creates previews only for PRs in the stack that include [render preview] in their title.

Each preview creates new resources that are billed according to their compute plans and other specs. If you use automatic previews, this change might increase your preview-related costs.

Learn more about previews in the documentation for service previews and preview environments.

]]> <![CDATA[Render Sandboxes now available in beta]]> https://render.com/changelog/render-sandboxes-now-available-in-beta 2026-11-11T00:00:00.000Z Now in public beta, use Render Sandboxes to spin up isolated, ephemeral compute environments for executing untrusted code, such as agent-generated apps and scripts.

Create and manage sandboxes programmatically using the Render CLI or the TypeScript and Python SDKs.

Each sandbox provides:

  • Isolated runtime: Run commands and manage files in a contained environment with its own filesystem.
  • Configurable compute: Choose from four compute plans with up to 8 CPU and 16 GB of RAM.
  • Indefinite execution: Run sandboxes for as long as you need. Configure separate timeouts for automatic suspension and termination, or disable both to run indefinitely.
  • Network controls: Restrict outbound traffic to specific HTTPS destinations, or block it entirely.
  • Reusable snapshots: Capture filesystem state or running processes, then restore that state in new sandboxes.

To create your first sandbox and execute a command:

  1. Install the latest version of the Render CLI.

  2. Spin up a sandbox with:

    # Create a sandbox and wait until it's running.
render sandboxes create --timeout=300 --wait

    Copy your new sandbox's ID from the command's output.

  3. Replace sbx-abc123 with your sandbox's ID in the following commands:

    # Execute a basic echo command.
render sandboxes exec sbx-abc123 -- echo hello from Render

# Terminate the sandbox when finished.
render sandboxes stop sbx-abc123 --confirm

Get started with Render Sandboxes in the documentation.

]]> <![CDATA[Reduced median first-build time for Docker-based previews by 45%]]> https://render.com/changelog/reduced-median-first-build-time-for-docker-based-previews-by-45 2026-11-11T00:00:00.000Z Docker-based service previews and preview environments now use the build cache from their base service’s most recent successful build. Previously, each preview’s first build started with an empty cache.

This optimization has reduced median first-build time for Docker-based previews by 45%:

Before this change (September 6 to October 28), median first-build time was 73 seconds. Since the optimization landed on October 29, the highest observed weekly median is 40 seconds.

Learn more about service previews and preview environments.

]]> <![CDATA[Reuse a build across multiple services]]> https://render.com/changelog/reuse-a-build-across-multiple-services 2026-11-10T00:00:00.000Z Now in private beta, build reuse enables you to build your code once, then deploy that build to multiple Render services:

By default, each Render service builds independently, even if their build configurations are identical. By reusing builds, you can maintain build consistency across services and reduce your total build pipeline usage.

You can share builds across web services, private services, background workers, and cron jobs.

To try build reuse and provide feedback during the private beta, request access.

]]> <![CDATA[Upcoming service preview and preview environment support for GitHub stacked PRs]]> https://render.com/changelog/upcoming-service-preview-and-preview-environment-support-for-github-stacked-prs 2026-11-04T00:00:00.000Z On November 18, 2026, Render will begin supporting separate service previews and preview environments for each pull request in a GitHub PR stack:

Currently, Render creates previews only for PRs that directly target your service's linked branch. This means that only the bottom PR in a stack can generate previews.

Beginning November 18, Render will apply your existing preview mode to all PRs in a stack:

  • Automatic: Render will create previews for each PR in the stack, except for any that include [skip preview] in their title.
  • Manual: Render will create previews only for PRs in the stack that include [render preview] in their title.

Each preview creates new resources that are billed according to their compute plans and other specs. If you use automatic previews, this change might increase your preview-related costs.

  • Learn more about previews in the documentation for service previews and preview environments.
  • To enable previews for stacked PRs sooner, reach out to our support team in the Render Dashboard.
]]> <![CDATA[Updated default versions of Node.js and Bun]]> https://render.com/changelog/updated-default-versions-of-node-js-and-bun 2026-10-22T00:00:00.000Z Newly created services that use Node.js or Bun now default to the following versions:

  • Node.js 24.22.1
  • Bun 1.4.4

You can always specify a different version of Node.js or Bun.

Existing services keep their original default versions to prevent breaking changes.

]]> <![CDATA[Added support for Bun canary builds]]> https://render.com/changelog/added-support-for-bun-canary-builds 2026-10-16T00:00:00.000Z Render now supports canary builds for Bun. Canary builds let you preview upcoming Bun features before they reach a stable release.

To use canary builds, do one of the following:

  • Set your service's BUN_VERSION environment variable to canary.
  • Add a .bun-version file to the root of your repo with the single line: canary.

Don't use Bun canary builds for production services. Canary builds are untested pre-releases. Learn more about setting your Bun version.

]]> <![CDATA[Added two Key Value plans and lowered prices for larger existing plans]]> https://render.com/changelog/added-two-key-value-plans-and-lowered-prices-for-larger-existing-plans 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z Render now supports two additional compute plans for Key Value instances:

  • 3 GB RAM with up to 3,000 simultaneous connections
  • 50 GB RAM with up to 50,000 simultaneous connections

We've also reduced pricing for existing Key Value compute plans that provide at least 1 GB RAM. The reduced pricing takes effect for all applicable Key Value instances starting October 1.

View all available plans and their latest pricing on the pricing page. Learn more about Render Key Value in the docs.

]]> <![CDATA[Added Blueprint support for Render Workflows]]> https://render.com/changelog/added-blueprint-support-for-render-workflows 2026-09-16T00:00:00.000Z You can now manage your workflow services using Blueprints, Render's infrastructure-as-code model.

Define workflows alongside other service types in your Blueprint YAML. Here's an example:

services:
  - type: workflow
    name: my-workflow
    runtime: python
    region: oregon
    repo: https://github.com/render-examples/render-workflows-examples-python
    branch: main
    rootDir: hello-world
    buildCommand: pip install -r requirements.txt
    startCommand: python main.py

Workflows support most of the same configuration fields as other service types, with exceptions noted in the Blueprint YAML Reference. Notably, you don't provide a plan field for workflows, because you instead specify compute plans per task directly in your code.

Note the following:

  • Workflows do not yet support preview environments, which skip replicating any workflows present in your Blueprint (other services are replicated as usual).
  • Render rejects a Blueprint that would create a workflow with the same name as an existing Blueprint-managed workflow in your workspace.

Learn more about Render Workflows in the documentation.
